source.title: Neural Architecture Search with Random Labels
source.authors: Xuan-Yang Zhang; Pengfei Hou; X. Zhang; Jian Sun

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Applies random labels in neural architecture search and reports results about the architectures selected, extending random-label work to the NAS setting. It does not directly test the versions’ claims about fitting random labels in standard networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports NAS search and downstream-task results using random labels. Those results measure architecture-search performance, not whether an individual network fits the training set with random labels, its training error or test error. No rows qualify for V1–V6. Mentioned results about networks fitting random labels in the introduction are attributed to prior work and are excluded.
record.test_reason: RLNAS trains a weight-sharing SuperNet with random labels as a tool for architecture search. Its results measure architecture ranking and performance after supervised retraining, without reporting fit to random labels, relative fitting time, or learning order. These results do not test V1–V6; the record's T3 classification should be T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that RLNAS can search using only random labels and discover architectures with performance comparable to or better than several supervised and unsupervised NAS methods, including transfer to detection and segmentation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random labels to train a weight-sharing SuperNet, then searches architectures using an angle-based convergence metric; this is a NAS procedure, not the original experiments on fitting random labels in standard deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: Random-label generation method affects search performance and transfer: methods assigning labels once generally perform better than per-iteration randomization; one per-iteration method is reported as unstable and poor at transfer. On ImageNet16-120, performance fluctuates greatly with few label categories (10–50).

fits_no_version.finding: With random-label SuperNet training, angle-based architecture rankings correlate with supervised performance: Kendall's tau is 0.5059, 0.5097, and 0.4716 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet16-120, respectively (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight changes during random-label SuperNet training can rank architectures by their subsequent supervised performance.

fits_no_version.finding: RLNAS discovers architectures achieving comparable or better supervised classification and downstream-task performance than several NAS baselines (Tables 1 and 3–11). These scores evaluate discovered architectures after supervised training, rather than accuracy on the random-label task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random labels can replace informative labels during architecture search when paired with the proposed angle metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Search performance depends on random-label generation: fixed labels generally perform better across datasets than labels regenerated each iteration; category count also affects search performance in some settings (Table 6 and Figure 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effectiveness of random-label architecture search depends on label-generation choices.

record.peer_reviewed: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (as stated in supplied metadata); the paper text does not specify the venue further.
record.problems: The paper does not report training error or test error on the random-label training task itself. Its reported accuracy results evaluate architectures discovered by the NAS procedure. Some category-count results are presented only in Figure 1 without numeric values in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were eligible: reported tables and figures concern search performance, ranking correlation, or downstream task performance, rather than the behaviors named by V1–V6. Introductory statements about deep networks fitting random labels cite prior work and are not the study's own results.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error and chance test error on completely random labels with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus true labels and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions. Weight-angle ranking does not measure these comparisons.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error across label-corruption fractions.
Whether regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it impairs true-label generalization.
Whether shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels during training.

record.verdict_notes: Keeping the result rows empty is appropriate. The omitted NAS results are explicitly declared in rows_left_out. Statements about networks fitting random labels in Section 3.2.1 are attributed to prior work and supply no independent evidence for V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit random training labels to near-zero training error, have chance test error, and do so without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training-time comparison for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Training fit and test error across corruption fractions.
Effects of regularization and augmentation on fitting random labels and true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels over training.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study uses random-label training without measuring random-label fitting error, relative fitting time, noise-dependent generalization, or learning order.

tranche.reason: Random-label SuperNet training is a tool for architecture search. Reported outcomes measure architecture ranking and downstream performance, without testing V1–V6.

source_check.notes: Section 4.2.1, Table 2, row D (RLNAS) confirms all three Kendall correlations against NAS-Bench-201 ground-truth performance rankings. These correlations do not measure successful fitting of random labels.
